title: Record of Entering Shu
subtitle: Lu You · Up the Yangtze Against the Current · Six Months to Kuizhou
description: Lu You (1125–1210), courtesy name Wuguan, sobriquet Fangweng, was born in Shanyin, Yuezhou (present-day Shaoxing, Zhejiang), the greatest poet of the Southern Song. In the sixth year of the Qiandao reign (1170), at the age of forty-six, Lu You was appointed Assistant Magistrate of Kuizhou. Departing from his hometown of Shanyin, he traveled up the Yangtze River against the current, reaching Kuizhou after one hundred and fifty-seven days. He recorded his journey in the six-volume Record of Entering Shu, capturing every scenic sight and historical relic along the way. This route follows Lu You's river journey along the Yangtze, visiting the nationally protected heritage sites that witnessed the poet's upstream voyage.

route.title: Record of Entering Shu: Lu You's Poetic Journey Up the Yangtze, Six Months to Kuizhou
route.intro:
The road took half a year to traverse, yet the rivers and mountains before me stretched into endless vistas.
On the eighteenth day of the intercalary fifth month of the sixth year of the Qiandao reign (1170), Lu You, aged forty-six, set out from Shanyin (present-day Shaoxing). He had spent several idle years at home, and finally a post had come—Assistant Magistrate of Kuizhou, a tiny, remote, utterly insignificant office. But Lu You did not complain. He packed his bags, gathered his family, hired a boat, and entered the Yangtze via the canal, beginning his long voyage upstream. The journey took a full one hundred and fifty-seven days. Lu You kept a diary every day—the mountains and waters he saw, the ancient sites he encountered, the stories he heard—all of it he wrote down. This is the Record of Entering Shu, one of the most beautiful travel diaries in all of Chinese literature. He was not merely traveling; he was surveying the world through the eyes of a poet—every ancient temple, every stone stele, every bend in the river, all were material for his verse. Let us follow Lu You's wake, from the waterways of Jiangnan to the depths of the Three Gorges, and feel, against the Yangtze's current, the solitude and soaring spirit of a poet.

stops.title: Stop One: Zhenjiang—Jiaoshan Stele Forest, a Floating Jade in the River
stops.content: On the twentieth day of the intercalary fifth month, Lu You entered the Yangtze and made his first stop at Zhenjiang. He could not wait to climb Jiaoshan, the islet in the river known as "a Floating Jade in the River," which had been a pilgrimage site for scholars and poets since the Eastern Han. What captivated Lu You most on Jiaoshan was the Jiaoshan Stele Forest, which together with the Xi'an Stele Forest forms the two great stele collections of north and south China. In his Record of Entering Shu, he devoted considerable space to describing the "Epitaph for a Buried Crane" (Yihe Ming) in the stele forest—a cliff-side inscription hailed as the "Ancestor of Large Characters," traditionally attributed to Tao Hongjing of the Southern Dynasties. "The strokes are bold and powerful, beyond the reach of later generations"—Lu You's judgment was decisive. He lingered long before the stele, perhaps thinking of his own checkered official career—the crane was a bird of freedom, yet he had to sail against the current toward a distant post. Jiaoshan also held many other cliff inscriptions from the Six Dynasties onward, which Lu You examined and recorded one by one. Across the Yangtze, Jinshan was faintly visible in the mist on the opposite bank—this was the first place on his journey that stirred his soul. Lu You's obsession with the Yihe Ming was no accident. This cliff inscription occupies an exalted position in the history of Chinese calligraphy—Huang Tingjian called it the "Ancestor of Large Characters" because it pioneered the unique style of "large characters." The inscription tells the mourning story of a master burying his crane: "The crane's lifespan is beyond reckoning; in the renchen year it was acquired at Huating, in the jiawu year it transformed at Zhufang"—the passing of a single crane elicited a masterpiece for the ages. In his Record of Entering Shu, Lu You wrote: "Only a few dozen characters of the Yihe Ming's broken stone remain today, yet the marvel of its brushwork could only be the work of the Right Army [Wang Xizhi]." Although modern scholars mostly attribute the work to Tao Hongjing, Lu You's judgment reflects the Southern Song literati's reverence for the "Sage of Calligraphy." The Jiaoshan Stele Forest became the finest in Jiangnan thanks to its unique geography—Jiaoshan is an islet surrounded by water on all sides in the Yangtze, difficult for warfare to reach, allowing inscriptions from successive dynasties to be safely preserved. From the Six Dynasties to the Qing, the forest holds nearly five hundred steles, of which the Yihe Ming, the "Ancestor of Large Characters," is merely the most brilliant pearl. Lu You lingered on Jiaoshan for an entire day, descending the mountain to his boat only at dusk. The sunset dyed the river gold; he looked back at Jiaoshan, that tiny "Floating Jade in the River" gradually disappearing into dusk—he knew that once he left, he might never see it again.

stops.title: Stop Two: Nanjing—The Six Dynasties, a Dream Broken by Birdsong
stops.content: Passing through Jiangning (present-day Nanjing), Lu You went ashore to visit Stone City. As a man of the Southern Song, Nanjing was for him not merely the ancient capital of the Six Dynasties, but a place of heartache—the great northern territories had fallen to the Jin, the Southern Song court was huddled south of the Yangtze, and Nanjing stood on the front line of the divided realm. In Nanjing, Lu You visited the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum at the foot of Zhongshan—though in his day the Ming Xiaoling did not yet exist; the area was home to Buddhist temples and Daoist shrines from the Six Dynasties. The soughing pines of Zhongshan filled his ears, and he wrote in his diary: "The atmosphere of Zhongshan is truly the finest south of the Yangtze"—that single word "finest" reveals his utter admiration for Nanjing's landscape. He ascended the city walls and gazed into the distance: the Yangtze like a silken ribbon, the Qinhuai like a sash. He wrote the eternally famous lines "Where hills bend, streams wind, and the pathway seems lost; in the shade of willows, flowers bloom, and another village appears"—though these lines were written later in his hometown of Shanyin, their conception was already brewing amid the landscapes of Nanjing. After Nanjing, his boat entered Anhui, where the river widened and green mountains rose on both banks. Lu You's feelings toward Nanjing were deeply complex. Jiankang (Nanjing) was the Song "temporary capital"—the Southern Song court had established its provisional government here, and Emperor Xiaozong had repeatedly planned northern expeditions from this city. In his Record of Entering Shu, Lu You specifically climbed the Phoenix Terrace on the banks of the Qinhuai River, where Li Bai had written "On Phoenix Terrace once phoenixes came to play; the phoenixes are gone, but the river still flows its way." Standing at the terrace site, Lu You felt the weight of history: the splendor of the Six Dynasties had scattered, the Later Ruler of the Southern Tang had been taken north as a captive, and now the Southern Song court was also huddled south of the Yangtze—"The vicissitudes of a thousand years, heard only in a fisherman's midnight song." In his Record of Entering Shu, Lu You noted a particular structure in Nanjing—"Stone City" (Shitoucheng), "the mountains surround the ancient kingdom on all sides, the tide beats against the empty city and returns in solitude." The red sandstone of the city wall foundation, worn by years of river erosion, formed an uneven, "ghost-face" texture, earning it the name "Ghost Face City." As Lu You stroked the stones polished smooth by river water, he may have thought of himself—a man of forty-six receiving only a minor post as Kuizhou Assistant Magistrate, like these stones, scoured by the Yangtze of fate for half a lifetime. But he was not dejected—"Lying in bed at night listening to wind and rain, I dream of iron-clad horses crossing frozen rivers"—even in his most despondent moments, he never forgot the dream of reconquering the northern heartland.

stops.title: Stop Three: Wuhan—Rivers Paying Homage, the Yellow Crane Gone
stops.content: In the seventh month, when the fiery weather arrived, Lu You's boat entered Ezhou (present-day Wuhan), where the Yangtze and Han Rivers converge. In his Record of Entering Shu, he wrote: "The rivers pay homage to the sovereign—a scene of majestic grandeur." The Yangtze and Han merge here, the water surface spreading for miles in a vast, misty expanse that opens the heart and mind. Lu You climbed Yellow Swan Mountain (Snake Mountain). The Yellow Crane Tower atop it had been destroyed by war, leaving only a Yuan-dynasty Victorious Image Pagoda standing alone by the river. He stood beneath the pagoda, gazing at the magnificent vista of "a lone sail's distant shadow vanishing into the blue sky, only the Yangtze flowing to the sky's edge." Perhaps he recalled Cui Hao's lines: "The ancients have ridden the yellow crane away; here only the Yellow Crane Tower remains." Though the tower was gone, the river remained, the poem remained, and the heart of the poet watching the lone sail depart remained. During his days in Wuhan, Lu You also crossed the river to Hanyang, climbing Tortoise Mountain and viewing the Qingchuan Pavilion. He was full of praise for the fertility and abundance of the Jianghan Plain—likely a rare stretch of ease for a man weary from exile. The Victorious Image Pagoda, built in the third year of the Yuan Zhizheng reign (1343), is a Tibetan Buddhist-style white stupa that did not yet exist in Lu You's time—yet he had already sensed the serene religious aura on Yellow Swan Mountain. In his Record of Entering Shu, he wrote: "Yellow Swan Mountain once had the Yellow Crane Tower, now destroyed by war. At the summit there is a Mendicant's Temple, with flourishing incense." This temple is one of the oldest Buddhist monasteries in Wuhan. Lu You paid his respects at the temple, then went to the mountaintop to gaze into the distance. The Yangtze and Han Rivers converged at his feet in a surging, majestic confluence, and the "rivers paying homage to the sovereign" grandeur temporarily made him forget the loneliness of his official career. Lu You also did something in Wuhan that many overlook—he visited the "Red Cliffs" remains along the riverbank. Although the true battlefield of the Red Cliffs is at Puqi (present-day Chibi), the "Red Bluff" on the Wuhan riverfront stirred the poet's heroic spirit. He wrote in his Record of Entering Shu: "Beneath the Red Cliffs Bluff, the river roars; the sheer cliffs rise a thousand feet." Though he did not explicitly mention Su Shi's "Red Cliffs Rhapsody," every reader cannot help but recall Dongpo's words: "The great river flows eastward, washing away the gallant figures of a thousand ages." Lu You and Su Shi—one of the Northern Song, one of the Southern—their souls were forever linked on the banks of the Yangtze.

stops.title: Stop Four: Yichang—The Three Wandering Immortals Cave, a Spiritual Encounter with Dongpo
stops.content: Passing through Jingzhou, the boat entered Xiling Gorge—the longest of the Three Gorges. On both banks, perilous peaks rose like sheer knife-cuts, and the river roared and surged. Aboard his boat, Lu You felt nature's most primal power. His descriptions of the Three Gorges in Record of Entering Shu are extraordinarily vivid—that sense of deep seclusion, where "even at noon in midsummer you cannot see the sun or moon," makes you feel as though he were not writing a travelogue but composing a long landscape poem. At the mouth of Xiling Gorge, there is a wondrous cave called the Three Wandering Immortals Cave (Sanyou Dong). When Lu You arrived, the Three Wandering Immortals Cave Cliff Inscriptions had already gained fame from the "former three wanderers"—Bai Juyi, Bai Xingjian, and Yuan Zhen of the Tang—and the "later three wanderers"—Su Xun, Su Shi, and Su Zhe of the Song. Lu You crawled into the cave and saw cliff walls densely covered with inscriptions from successive dynasties—among them, the handwriting of Su Shi, whom he had admired all his life. He stood solemnly before Su Shi's inscription, as if holding a conversation across the ages with that great literary giant. The cave is not large, but "a mountain need not be high to be famous for its immortals." Beside the traces of his predecessors, Lu You also left his own inscription—today, the cave's stone carvings, superimposed from the Tang dynasty to the Republic of China, form the most precious cultural legacy of Sanyou Dong. Lu You's exploration of the cave was nearly archaeological—in his Record of Entering Shu, he noted the position and content of every inscription. Bai Juyi's running script was "vigorous and forceful," Su Shi's regular script "plump and mellow," while Lu You's own inscription was in his finest running-cursive script: "On a certain day of the seventh month of the sixth year of Qiandao, Lu You of Shanyin visited this place." The cave is small, but its stalactites take a thousand forms, and the stalagmites glisten with droplets of water—"strike them and the sound is like a chime of jade." Lu You spent an entire afternoon in the cave—perhaps waiting for rain, or perhaps simply savoring the most serene moments of his journey through the Three Gorges. What makes Sanyou Dong most moving is not the cave itself, but the stories behind the names that left their marks here. Bai Juyi, banished from the capital to be Sima of Jiangzhou, passed through this way. Su Shi, exiled to Huangzhou for the Crow Terrace Poetry Case, came this way too. Lu You, his career thwarted, was being sent to remote Kuizhou—three disheartened men from three different ages, forming a "league of the disheartened" across time and space in the Three Wandering Immortals Cave. Yet none of them was crushed by fate: Bai Juyi wrote the "Pipa Song" in Jiangzhou, Su Shi wrote the "Red Cliffs Rhapsodies" in Huangzhou, and Lu You wrote the Record of Entering Shu in Kuizhou—what they left in Sanyou Dong was not complaint, but serenity in the face of adversity.

stops.title: Stop Five: White Emperor City—Liu Bei's Entrustment, Li Bai's Swift Boat
stops.content: Passing through Wu Gorge and Qutang Gorge, Lu You finally arrived at Kuimen—the western gateway of the Three Gorges. On both sides, sheer cliffs rose like gates; the Yangtze squeezed through a canyon only a few dozen meters wide—the most magnificent stretch of the river. Above Kuimen on White Emperor Mountain stood the millennia-old White Emperor City. Lu You climbed White Emperor City and recounted in his Record of Entering Shu the historical allusions of this place: Gongsun Shu declaring himself emperor in the late Western Han; Liu Bei entrusting his son to Zhuge Liang after defeat in the Three Kingdoms; Li Bai's "Departing White Emperor City in the morning amid clouds of many a hue, returning to Jiangling in a single day—a thousand miles passed through"—a single small mountain, layered with too much history. Lu You lingered before the steles in the city—"having examined poems and inscriptions by ancient worthies, no less than several hundred"—White Emperor City was the most densely inscribed spot in the Three Gorges. Lu You himself dashed off a poem on White Emperor City—the bold spirit of "riding a donkey through Sword Gate in the fine rain" was already germinating here. Looking down from White Emperor City, Kuimen stood majestic beneath heaven, the Yangtze roaring and surging like a giant dragon—Lu You knew that his destination, Kuizhou, was only the last few dozen miles of water away.

stops.title: Stop Six: Kuizhou—End of the Journey, Zhang Fei's Temple, Loyalty Through the Ages
stops.content: In early winter, the boat finally reached Kuizhou (present-day Fengjie, Chongqing). One hundred and fifty-seven days of upstream navigation had come to an end. On the last pages of his Record of Entering Shu, Lu You recorded the landscapes and customs of Kuizhou. Though he was merely taking up a minor post, his patriotic fervor had not diminished in the slightest. Downstream from Kuizhou, in Yunyang County, the Zhang Huanhou Temple stood on the cliff by the river, built to commemorate the fierce Three Kingdoms general Zhang Fei. During his tenure in Kuizhou, Lu You likely visited this temple. After Zhang Fei was assassinated, his head drifted down the river to Yunyang, where the local populace built a temple in his honor—the four characters "Wind and River Clear" are carved on the temple's facade to this day. The temple housed a forest of steles, including the handwritings of Yan Zhenqing and Su Shi. Interestingly, Lu You styled himself "Fangweng" (the Recluse), while Zhang Fei was the most famous "rough-and-ready man" of the Three Kingdoms—yet what Lu You felt before Zhang Fei's temple was an aura of "loyalty and righteousness." The scholar bows to the warrior—a shared sigh across a thousand years. Lu You served three years in Kuizhou, and though his office was small, he never forgot the dream of recovering the central plains—"On the day the king's army pacifies the central plains, do not forget to tell your father at the family sacrifice"—this deathbed poem was the best footnote to his lifelong aspirations. Zhang Huanhou Temple, also known as Zhang Fei Temple, took its name from "Huanhou," the posthumous title conferred by Shu Han after Zhang Fei's death. Lu You's description of this temple in Record of Entering Shu is filled with emotion in every word: "The temple faces the great river, looking across the water toward Kuizhou City." The temple directly faces Kuimen, and the four characters "Wind and River Clear" are inscribed high on the cliff, facing the Yangtze, as if still guarding the territory of Shu Han. What moved Lu You most in the temple was a stele by Yan Zhenqing—the most principled calligrapher and loyal minister of the Tang, who "alone defended Pingyuan Commandery during the An Lushan Rebellion, the rebel army unable to take it." Seeing Yan Zhenqing's stele in Zhang Fei's temple, two iron-willed souls met across four centuries. In 2003, due to the impoundment of the Three Gorges Dam, Zhang Fei Temple was relocated in its entirety—craftsmen numbered every brick, tile, and stele, dismantling and rebuilding them thirty-two kilometers upstream at a site identical to the original. This was one of the largest relocation projects in the history of Chinese architecture. The four characters "Wind and River Clear" still face the Yangtze. If Lu You's spirit watches from above, he might well write another volume of Record of Entering Shu for this great "temple relocation drama"—for his Kuizhou and his Zhang Fei Temple have both found eternal life in the roar of the Yangtze's waves.
